title: The Flickering Family Photo
markdown:
The Merryweathers lived in a house that overflowed with laughter and smelled of freshly baked biscuits. And in that house lived two very special pals: Levi the otter, and Pansy the paper crane.

Levi was an otter of lots of splish-splash. He would zoom through the garden, whiskers twitching, always ready for a game of chase-the-bubble or find-the-shinest-pebble. He would slosh and tumble, leaving little puddles of otter-joy everywhere he went. And Pansy? She was a paper crane, folded with the brightest most cheerful paper you ever did see. She would perch on Levi’s head. Or she would flutter gently near the window. Her paper wings caught the sun like tiny stained-glass windows. They were the very best of friends, a whiskery whirlwind and a papery whisper.

The Merryweathers were a delightful bunch. Mum, who always smelled faintly of cinnamon and kindness. Dad, who had a laugh that rumbled like distant thunder. Lily, a whirlwind of pigtails and giggles. Leo, eyes as wide and curious as a startled fawn. They had a photograph hanging right in the hall, a grand old-fashioned sort of picture, framed in swirly gold that glinted like treasure. It showed the whole family, smiling their very best smiles. But every time someone looked at it, something really strange happened. One of the children, sometimes Lily, sometimes Leo, would simply vanish from the photograph. Gone like a whisper of smoke. And then, a moment later, they would blink back in, looking perfectly normal and wondering what all the fuss was about, but the photo would be wrong. It was like a game of hide-and-seek, but the game was the picture itself.

"Goodness me, that is funny," Mum would say, her brow furrowed like a rumpled napkin.
"My goodness gracious, look at that," Dad would exclaim, his voice a low rumble of surprise.
Lily would frown, pigtails standing straight up with confusion. Leo would tug at his shirt, looking a bit wobbly, wide eyes darting from the photo to his own hands. This happened every single time they glanced at the picture. It was as if the photo just could not make up its mind who to keep.

Levi’s tummy did a somersault, a scaredy-cat somersault, and his whiskers drooped like sad spaghetti. He nudged Pansy gently with his nose.

Levi and Pansy, who were usually busy planning their next game of who-can-splash-the-highest or find-the-most-magnificent-mushroom, noticed the sad droop of the Merryweathers’ shoulders. This was not right. Laughter should be tumbling out of the Merryweather house, not whispers of worry and the quiet tap-tap-tap of anxious fingers.

"What is wrong with the picture, Pansy?" Levi asked, sleek fur rippling with concern. He tilted his head, whiskers practically vibrating.
Pansy tilted her paper head, sunlight making her bright colours gleam. "The picture is wobbly, Levi. Like it is trying to decide something important. Like it has a wiggly thought it cannot shake loose."

They decided, right then and there, with a solemn nod from Levi and a determined flutter of Pansy’s wings, that they would solve the mystery of the flickering family. Their mission: make the photograph stop flickering and be a happy solid memory. Their reward: happy Merryweathers once more, full of the usual delightful chaos.

They asked everyone they knew. The garden gnome just grunted, his mossy beard giving nothing away. Gnomes are notoriously bad at solving photo-follies. The grumpy robin sang a very rude song about worms and the general foolishness of humans. Some birds have no manners. But then, near the ancient oak tree at the edge of the garden, they met Cadfael, an ancient wise old squirrel who had seen everything. Cadfael had a tail so bushy it looked like a furry cloud, and eyes that sparkled with knowing. He munched on a nut, his bushy tail twitching like a question mark.

"Ah, the photograph," Cadfael chuffed, his voice raspy like dry leaves. "A tricky thing, those old picture-makers. They needed such a long time to get the shot just right back then. People had to hold perfectly still, for ages. Imagine that. Like a statue, but awake." He winked a tiny beady eye. "The secret," he whispered, leaning closer, his breath smelling of acorns and damp earth, "is stillness. Absolute, unwavering, joyful stillness. The photograph needs to feel that calm moment to remember it properly. It is like trying to catch a butterfly with clumsy hands. You have to be gentle and patient."

Stillness? Levi’s whiskers drooped. He was the king of wiggles. He had once tried to be still for five whole seconds while Mum was trying to tie his shoelaces and ended up doing a spectacular somersault by accident, scattering shoelaces everywhere. And Cadfael mentioned joyful stillness? That sounded even harder than trying to catch a sunbeam.

Levi and Pansy had a big think. They sat under the oak tree, Pansy perched on a low branch, Levi tracing patterns in the dirt with his paw. How could they make the Merryweathers be perfectly still and joyful, all at the same time? It was like trying to teach a fish to fly. If they did not figure it out soon, the Merryweathers might just forget how to smile properly forever. The thought made his tail give a nervous thump-thump on the ground.

Suddenly Levi’s nose twitched. He smelled something delicious. Freshly baked, still-warm, honey-glazed salmon. Mum’s special treat, the kind that made his tummy do a happy dance all by itself. "Ooh. Salmon." His mind was already half-way to the kitchen, picturing the flaky pink goodness.

Pansy whispered from her perch, paper wings giving a little flutter of warning. "Levi. Remember Cadfael. Stillness. Joyful stillness."

Levi jolted back, shaking his head so hard his ears flapped. Oh, right. The photograph. He almost let his tummy rumble the solution away. This was the tricky bit Cadfael talked about, the choice that made you want to go back to your old ways, to that delicious easy thing. He had to choose the mission over the immediate glorious fishy delight. He focused. He imagined the fish, then he imagined Lily’s giggle, and Leo’s surprised delight. He took a deep breath. "Right. Salmon can wait. We need a plan."

Their plan was a masterpiece of otter-and-crane ingenuity. It involved Lily’s favourite bouncy ball, a bright red one that Leo loved to chase; Leo’s giggliest rubber duck, the one that squeaked like a tiny surprised mouse; and a very carefully placed daisy chain, woven by Pansy herself, to sit on the mantelpiece. They explained it all to Mum and Dad, voices full of earnestness.

"We need everyone to stand exactly as you are, for just a little bit," Pansy whispered, paper wings fluttering with importance. "And think happy thoughts," Levi added, though his own thoughts were currently full of that salmon, doing a little jig of its own in his imagination. He shook his head fiercely, trying to banish the fishy thoughts. "Happy thoughts. Like finding an extra shiny stone that glitters in the sun."

So it was time. The sunbeam in the hall was just right. Mum and Dad lined up with Lily and Leo, positioning themselves where the photograph usually hung. Levi and Pansy stood near the camera, a peculiar whiskery papery duo, ready to observe. Everyone took their place. Mum smiled her kind smile. Dad chuckled a low rumbling chuckle. Lily squeezed her rubber duck so it gave a tiny squeak. Leo held his bouncy ball, eyes wide with anticipation.

"Now," called Dad, holding up the old-fashioned camera, a curious contraption of brass and glass that clicked and whirred like a clockwork beetle.

As the camera began its long slow click-click-click, preparing to capture the moment, Leo suddenly felt a tickle in his tummy, the same wobbly feeling he got when he saw the vanishing child in the photo. He wanted to squirm. He wanted to peek. He wanted to check if he was still there. He tensed, little legs preparing to wobble right out of the picture.

Then a tiny papery whisper brushed his ear, light as a falling feather. "Hold on, Leo. You are perfectly you. Just breathe. Think of your favourite game."

Levi, meanwhile, felt his paws twitching, ready to do a little dance of excitement that the photo was almost done. He could practically taste the salmon now. He swallowed hard, sleek fur feeling suddenly tight and warm against his skin. The imagined scent of salmon, flaky and rich, warred with the faint comforting smell of damp garden soil. He stood utterly still, paws planted firmly on the cool dewy grass, not a wiggle in his whiskery body. The camera’s slow whirr was a low hum in his ears, a sound that promised a solid happy future.

Click. Whizz. Then silence. The mechanical whirring stopped.

The family blinked. They looked at the photograph. And there they were. All four of them. Perfectly still. Perfectly happy. No one was missing. Lily and Leo were right there, beaming, their smiles bright and solid.

Lily let out a little squeal, a sound like tiny bells chiming in the breeze. Leo giggled, a bubbling sound that made Levi’s whiskers twitch with pure joy. Mum and Dad hugged each other, faces shining brighter than any gold frame, worries melting away like snow in sunshine.

The photograph was not flickering anymore. It was a beautiful solid memory of a complete family, captured for all time. Levi the otter, who had held still despite his wiggles, and Pansy the paper crane, who had offered a whisper of courage, looked at each other with quiet triumph. They had not vanished. They had not moved. They had helped.

And as for that salmon? There was plenty to go around later, and everyone, even the very still Levi, agreed it was the most delicious meal ever. The gold frame glinted. The hall smelled of biscuits again. Cadfael, somewhere in the oak, was probably still chewing.
